title: Best Golf Balls UK
short: Premium golf balls compared on launch-monitor data and on-course testing, from Titleist Pro V1 to a lower-priced Mizuno that matched the market leaders.
intro: A golf ball's real test is measured spin, speed and distance, then how it behaves on a real course. This guide compares balls tested by Golf Monthly's Sam De'Ath, a professional with over a decade in the industry, who hit 20 shots each with a sand wedge, 7-iron and driver on a Foresight launch monitor in their Performance Lab, played a round with each ball, and ran a five-shot driver dispersion test against the leading ball. The page lists nine balls; the seven shown in full are covered here.

products.name: Pro V1 (2025)
products.best_for: Golfers who want complete tee-to-green performance
products.key_spec: Three-piece, cast urethane elastomer cover, 388 tetrahedral dimple design
products.summary: Golf Monthly's top pick for total performance, with a soft, responsive feel and a little extra distance off the tee, particularly with mid irons. In testing it flew consistently and stably, cutting through the wind with no major distance drop-off into headwinds and little effect from crosswinds, while excelling on approach shots. Lower-spin players may get better performance from the Pro V1x.
pros: Improved distance, particularly with mid irons
Strong, stable ball flight in the wind
cons: Low-spin players may get better performance from the Pro V1x

products.name: Pro X
products.best_for: Golfers who want premium performance at a lower price
products.key_spec: Three-piece, also available as REVA for women, noticeably cheaper than premium rivals
products.summary: Golf Monthly's tester was 'blown away': the Pro X flew further than the Srixon Z-Star XV and seven yards longer than the previous-generation Titleist Pro V1x in testing. Iron flight was high but controlled and consistent, with a responsive feel on wedges and a soft touch on the green, at a noticeably lower price than the best premium balls. The only real downside is that Mizuno isn't a brand golfers associate with premium balls.

specs.Colours: Yellow and white (REVA version for women)
specs.Compared with rivals: Seven yards longer than previous Pro V1x in testing

pros: Exceptional value given ball speed and carry distance
cons: Not a brand many golfers associate with premium balls

products.name: Chrome Tour (2026)
products.best_for: Skilled players who want a soft feel without losing distance
products.key_spec: Four-piece, Tour Fast Mantle, Advanced Seamless Tour Aero dimples, low long-game spin
products.summary: Golf Monthly found this delivers low long-game spin and a lower iron spin profile, prioritising speed and flight stability, yet still reaches a high peak height, letting skilled players flight shots without losing distance. It felt soft without compromising distance and around the greens gave impressive 'drop-and-stop' spin for delicate wedge shots, though it may not suit golfers with slower swing speeds.
pros: Solid spin with chip and pitch shots
Ideal for those wanting a lower iron flight
cons: May not suit golfers with slower swing speeds

products.name: TP5 (2026)
products.best_for: Golfers who want a soft, stable ball that resists ballooning in wind
products.key_spec: Five-piece, Tour Flight dimple pattern, cast urethane cover, ball speeds close to 168mph in testing
products.summary: Golf Monthly found the new Tour Flight pattern stops the ballooning criticised on the previous model, with exceptional stability in the wind. Driver ball speeds reached close to 168mph, taking the tester over 300 yards, while it still felt softer than ever, and around the green the cast urethane cover gave high spin and confident chipping. High launch may not suit everyone.

specs.Colours: White and yellow (Pix design also available)

cons: High launch may not suit everyone

products.name: Z-Star Diamond (2025)
products.best_for: Golfers who want distance plus high approach and wedge spin
products.key_spec: Three-piece, lower trajectory and spin than the Z-Star XV, played on Tour by Brooks Koepka and Shane Lowry
products.summary: Golf Monthly found the Diamond kept up with the longer Z-Star XV off the tee while producing a lower trajectory and spin, good for windy conditions. It stands out with irons, spinning over 1,000rpm more than the Z-Star and 700rpm more than the Z-Star XV on a full sand wedge, and finds a middle ground between the soft Z-Star and the firmer XV. It perhaps lacks a premium look to match the performance.

specs.Wedge spin measured: Over 1,000rpm more than Z-Star, 700rpm more than Z-Star XV

cons: Perhaps doesn't have the premium look to match the performance

products.name: Pro V1x (2025)
products.best_for: Golfers who want a firmer, faster, lower-spinning premium ball
products.key_spec: Four-piece, faster off the tee and lower spinning than the previous version, favoured by professionals
products.summary: Golf Monthly saw a 0.5mph ball speed increase over the 2023 model, with carry up three yards and total distance up four, and could carry trees and hazards that previously needed a top strike. It flies as strongly as anything on the market with good stopping power into greens and strong wind performance, though it feels noticeably firmer than the regular Pro V1, which some will not prefer.
cons: Some may prefer the softer feel of the Pro V1

products.name: TP5x (2026)
products.best_for: Golfers chasing maximum ball speed and distance with a piercing flight
products.key_spec: Five-piece, TaylorMade's lowest-spinning, fastest five-layer tour ball, micro-coated dimples
products.summary: Golf Monthly saw ball speed gains over the previous model in their Performance Lab, combined with low spin for a penetrating, consistent flight and good rollout outdoors. The low-spin theme continues with irons, giving a shallower descent that suits soft greens more than very firm ones, and the distance comes with a firmer feel and less check when chipping than the TP5.

specs.Colours: White and yellow (Pix design also available)

cons: May spin a little low for slower swing speeds
Slightly firm and less check when chipping and pitching

guide.q: Which is the number one golf ball?
guide.a: Statistically the Titleist Pro V1 and Pro V1x are the most used balls on Tour, but top professionals also play the TaylorMade TP5 and TP5x, Callaway Chrome Tour and Srixon Z-Star models. Golf Monthly's point is that no single ball dominates, so the best ball depends on your own game, not a universal ranking.

guide.q: Do golf balls really make a difference?
guide.a: Yes: spin, launch and feel all change how the ball responds to your strike, and the same ball performs differently for a tour player and a 15-handicapper. Most brands make several models, so it's worth testing a couple to find your match.

Top-tier ranges often offer a softer standard model and a firmer, lower-spinning companion for more driver control, such as the Pro V1 and Pro V1x or the TP5 and TP5x here. Golf Monthly advises trying both from various distances to establish your own preference.

guide.q: Is a premium urethane ball worth the extra money?
guide.a: Urethane covers give better spin control and feel but cost substantially more. Golf Monthly suggests experimenting to see whether the performance gain justifies the price for your skill level, or whether a good mid-price ball, or a lower-priced option like the Mizuno Pro X here, gives enough performance for the money.
